pages.text:
UNITED STATES OF AMERICA 
BEFORE THE 
FEDERAL ENERGY REGULATORY COMMISSION 
 
PJM Interconnection, L.L.C. 
 
Docket No. ER26-3380-000 
 
MOTION FOR LEAVE TO ANSWER, 
AND ANSWER, OF 
THE ATTORNEY GENERAL OF THE COMMONWEALTH OF KENTUCKY 
 
Pursuant to Rules 212 and 213 of the Commission’s Rules of Practice and Procedure, 18 
C.F.R. §§ 385.212 and 385.213 (2025),1 the Attorney General of the Commonwealth of Kentucky 
(“Kentucky Attorney General” or “Attorney General”)2 hereby moves for leave to answer, and 
answers, comments on and protests of the July 31, 2026 filing by PJM Interconnection, L.L.C. 
(“PJM”) in this proceeding.3 
I. 
MOTION FOR LEAVE TO ANSWER 
Rule 213(a)(2) of the Commission’s Rules of Practice and Procedure generally prohibits 
answers to protests and other pleadings unless otherwise ordered by the decisional authority. The 
Kentucky Attorney General is authorized by statute to represent the interests of ratepayers in the 
Commonwealth of Kentucky and through this Answer offers its comments on the comments on 
and protests of the PJM Reliability Backstop Procurement (“RBP”) Filing.4 Good cause justifies 
the Commission’s granting this motion and accepting this Answer because the Answer provides 
 
1 18 C.F.R. §§ 385.212 and 385.213 (2026). 
2 The Kentucky Attorney General submitted a timely, doc-less motion to intervene in this proceeding on August 6, 
2026. 
3 PJM Interconnection, L.L.C., Docket No. ER26-3380-000, “Reliability Backstop Procurement to Address Resource 
Adequacy Concerns Stemming from Large Loads” (filed July 31, 2026) (“PJM RBP Filing”). 
4 KRS 367.150(8).

2 
information that may assist the Commission in its decision-making process and ensures a complete 
record.5 For these reasons, the Commission should accept this Answer. 
II. 
COMMENTS 
On August 21, 2026, East Kentucky Power Cooperative, LLC (“EKPC”) filed a protest in 
this docket. EKPC’s protest states several important concerns related to the RBP proposed by 
PJM.6 The Attorney General is equally concerned that steps should be taken to ensure that 
ratepayers are protected from the potential unjust and unreasonable cost allocation that could occur 
under the proposal. 
Of particular concern is whether Load Serving Entities who have met their obligations are 
protected from cost allocation in the event of default by the cost causer.  As detailed on pages 11, 
et seq, of the EKPC protest and in the Testimony of Adam Bednarczyk, the potential appears to 
exist for inappropriate cost shifting in the instance of default by responsible entities.  This potential 
is exacerbated by the lack of protection for Reliability Pricing Model entities who have prudently 
planned to fully serve their load. Under the RBP proposal, it does not appear that PJM 
appropriately decrements the target, or otherwise provides sufficient offsets, for utilities who have 
already taken appropriate actions to serve their load.7   
In general, the Kentucky Attorney General is concerned with the potential for others to free 
ride on the prudent resource adequacy decisions made by Load Serving Entities in Kentucky.  By 
allocating these costs unjustly, Kentucky utilities who have steel in the ground to serve their load

because they provided information that assisted the Commission in its decision-making process); PJM 
Interconnection, L.L.C., 189 FERC ¶ 61,110 at P 22 (2024) (accepting answers to protests and answers because they 
assisted the Commission in its decision-making process); Potomac-Appalachian Transmission Highline, LLC, 140 
FERC ¶ 61,229 at P 102 (2012) (accepting answer to an answer because it provided material evidence that corrected 
the record and informed the Commission’s decision-making process). 
6 See Protest of East Kentucky Power, Inc. filed August 21, 2026. 
7 Id. at 13-14, 28, et seq.

3 
could effectively be required to fund redundant resources from which they do not earn an 
additional reliability benefit. These concerns are particularly striking given that these costs could 
continue to compound over the 15-year term of the agreement, resulting in large potential penalties 
to utilities who have planned their systems prudently. Thus, great effort should be made to ensure 
that ratepayers are protected from unjust and unreasonable cost shifting that could occur pursuant 
to the foreseeable consequences of PJM’s RBP proposal. Importantly, doing otherwise would run 
afoul of the President’s Ratepayer Protection Pledge, which prohibits such cost shifting.8 
FERC simply must not allow the RBP to proceed unless reasonable assurance is provided 
that Kentucky ratepayers will be held harmless from the costs caused by others, whether those 
costs are driven by usage or insufficient planning.   
 
RUSSELL COLEMAN 
ATTORNEY GENERAL
